newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends at record high, bonds rally, dollar dips on data.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends at record high, bonds rally, dollar dips on data.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed at a record high, bonds rallied and the dollar fell on Thursday as a key jobs report improved chances that the Federal Reserve would hold U.S. interest rates steady.
Gold prices slumped to a 12-year low after news that the Australian central bank had sold 167 metric tons of gold reserves in recent months.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 100.43 points, or 1.29 percent, at 7,895.81, eclipsing its June 20 record close of 7,796.51. For the week, the blue-chip index was up 208.09 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues swamped declines 1,976 to 752 on volume of 374 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The broad rally also lifted secondary indexes to record levels.
The market closed early at 1 p.m. EDT/1700 GMT prior to Friday's Independence Day holiday.
Wall Street was in a bullish mood after fresh employment and wage data offered further evidence that the economy's growth remains moderate and inflation remains at bay.
The Labour Department said the jobless rate rose to 5.0 percent in June from a 24-year low of 4.8 percent in May.
In addition, monthly job growth and hourly wage increases were slightly lower than forecast.
Analysts said the data, which came one day after the Fed voted to hold interest rates steady, diminished chances for future increases.
"The economic backdrop at this point appears to be remarkable," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
"Inflation is nowhere to be found and investors are beginning to sense the August Fed meeting may also be one where rates are held in check," he said.
Analysts also detected a seasonal note in the market's performance, pointing out that the Independence Day holiday has produced more than its share of market fireworks in the past.
The 30-year U.S. Treasury bond soared almost one full point, lowering its yield to 6.62 percent from 6.71 percent Wednesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The dollar fell to 113.82 Japanese yen from 114.50 late Wednesday. It settled at 1.7535 German marks, just below its previous closing rate of 1.7550.
At the Commodity Exchange in New York, gold for August delivery closed down $7.10 an ounce at $325.20 after setting a new life-of-contract low at $324.00.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices ended sharply lower on news that Iraq had moved a step closer to resuming oil sales under its deal with the United Nations.

Crude oil for August delivery closed 78 cents lower at $19.56 a barrel. Refined products tracked crude, with August gasoline closing down 1.37 cents at a gallon at 57.92 cents and August heating oil down 2.16 cents at 52.76 a gallon.

At New York's Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, cocoa prices fell sharply for a third consecutive day as speculators cashed in positions ahead of the long U.S. holiday weekend on sentiment that a month-long rally had ended.
September cocoa closed $52 lower at $1,562 per metric ton. The contract has dropped 9 percent over the last three days.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices fell on excellent harvest progress for winter wheat and reports of excellent wheat yields, especially in the key U.S. hard red winter wheat state of Kansas.
September wheat closed at $3.27-1/2, down 5 cents a bushel, after setting a life-of-contract low at $3.27.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,831.7, up 80.3 points, or 1.69 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,121.41, down 75.01 points, or 0.37 percent.
